cues.text: We now turn to the third topic in this study session: automation in digital transformation.
Let us start with a question.

When an organisation digitises its work, what happens to the repetitive tasks that people do again and again, such as copying data between systems, checking forms against rules, or routing requests to the right person?
Automation is the use of technology to carry out such tasks with less manual effort.
There are several kinds, and it helps to keep them distinct.
The first is robotic process automation, usually called RPA.
It uses software bots to perform repetitive, rule-based interactions, often through existing interfaces.
The bot works much as a person would: it opens screens, reads fields, types values and clicks buttons.
Because it works through the interfaces that already exist, an organisation can often automate a task without rebuilding the underlying system.
The key words are repetitive and rule-based.
If the steps are the same each time and the rules are clear, a bot can follow them.
The second is workflow automation.
This coordinates tasks and approvals.
Think of a leave request that goes to a supervisor, then to human resources, then is recorded.
The workflow moves the work to the right person at the right time.
The third is business process automation.
It is broader.
It redesigns and automates whole processes rather than single tasks.
Note the word redesigns: the process itself is reconsidered, not just sped up.
The fourth is industrial automation, which controls physical equipment, such as machines on a production line.
Then we have intelligent automation, which combines artificial intelligence with automation.
It is used for tasks involving uncertain inputs, classification or adaptive decisions.
Ordinary automation follows fixed rules.
When the input is messy, varied or ambiguous, rules alone are not enough, and AI contributes the ability to interpret, classify or adapt.
The source gives a table with three columns: Example, Automation, and AI contribution.
Please look at the accompanying table as we go through it row by row.
Row one is invoice processing.
The automation routes, validates and records the invoice.
The AI contribution is to extract fields from varied documents.
Invoices arrive in many layouts, so AI reads them and pulls out the relevant fields, and the automation handles the routing, validation and recording.
Row two is customer support.
The automation opens and routes tickets.
The AI contribution is to interpret language and classify intent.
In other words, the AI works out what the customer is actually asking for, and the automation sends the ticket on its way.
Row three is manufacturing.
The automation controls scheduled machine operations.
The AI contribution is to predict equipment fault.
The machines run to schedule under automated control, while AI looks for signs that a fault is likely to occur.
Row four is banking.
The automation executes a defined verification workflow.
The AI contribution is to score unusual transaction patterns.
The verification steps are fixed, while the AI assigns scores to transactions that look unusual.
Notice the pattern across all four rows.
Automation executes the defined steps.
AI handles the part that involves uncertainty, language, prediction or pattern recognition.
Now let us consider why organisations adopt automation, and what can go wrong.
The benefits listed are speed, consistency, lower repetitive effort, scalability, auditability, cost reduction, and the ability to focus staff on higher-value tasks.
Auditability means that automated steps can leave a record of what was done, which helps with checking and accountability.
Scalability means volume can grow without a matching growth in manual effort.
But the source is equally clear about the risks.
These are: automating a broken process, brittle integrations, security exposure, hidden costs, worker displacement, model errors and overreliance.
Automating a broken process simply produces the wrong results faster.
Brittle integrations are connections between systems that break easily when something changes.
Security exposure arises because bots and integrations often hold access to systems and data.
Hidden costs are costs that do not appear in the first estimate.
Worker displacement concerns the people whose tasks are taken over.
Model errors are mistakes made by AI components.
And overreliance means trusting the automation more than its performance justifies.
A good digital leader weighs both lists, not just the first.
So how should an organisation proceed?
The source gives a sequence.
Start with process mapping and baseline measurements.
You must understand how the work is done now, and measure it, before you change it.
Next, identify repetitive, high-volume tasks, because these offer the greatest potential gain.
Then remove unnecessary steps.
This connects back to the risk of automating a broken process: simplify first, automate second.
Then define exception paths, meaning what happens when a case does not fit the normal rules.
Then select the appropriate automation, since the right choice among RPA, workflow, process or industrial automation, or intelligent automation, depends on the task.
Pilot before scaling, so that problems appear on a small scale.
Monitor failures and maintain fallback routes, so work can continue if the automation stops.
And remember this warning: a bot that fails silently can create more work than a manual process.
If nobody notices that it has failed, errors pile up unseen and must be found and corrected later.
Let us finish with the worked example, and I will take it step by step.
An organisation handles 10,000 invoices per month.
Manually, each invoice takes 6 minutes.
So 10,000 times 6 minutes is 60,000 minutes.
Dividing by 60 gives 1,000 hours of manual work each month.
Now consider the automated version.
Automated processing leaves 15% of invoices requiring review.
Fifteen percent of 10,000 is 1,500 invoices.
Each review still takes 6 minutes, so 1,500 times 6 is 9,000 minutes, which is 150 hours.
In addition, there are 100 hours each month for monitoring and maintenance of the automation.
So the total labour time after automation is 150 plus 100, which is 250 hours.
The net labour time reduction is 1,000 minus 250, which is 750 hours.
As a share of the original 1,000 hours, that is 75%.
Now pay close attention to the qualifications the source attaches.
This result assumes comparable quality and no additional hidden work.
And it does not directly establish savings.
A reduction in hours is not the same as a reduction in money.
To judge the real benefit, you must also account for licences, integration, staffing, exceptions and error costs.
The 750 hours is a measure of labour time, and a full financial case needs those further costs included.
To summarise: automation takes several forms, from RPA to industrial automation.
Intelligent automation adds AI where inputs are uncertain.
The benefits are real, but so are the risks.
And sound practice is to map and measure, simplify, plan for exceptions, pilot, monitor, and keep fallback routes in place.
